newsitem.title: USA: Test may give early prediction of prostate cancer.
newsitem.headline: Test may give early prediction of prostate cancer.

text.p: A new blood test holds promise of predicting possible cases of prostate cancer up to 10 years before the disease can be diagnosed, a six-year jump on current methods, U.S. scientists reported on Tuesday.

The new test involves a different way of monitoring the enzyme PSA -- prostate specific antigen -- in a man's blood, according to researchers at the National Institute on Ageing and the Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine.

"Currently, most physicians test for total PSA only, which when measured repeatedly over time, can predict prostate cancer up to four years before clinical diagnosis," Dr. James Fozard of the ageing institute said in a statement.

"This study, however, shows that measuring the ratio of free to total PSA repeatedly over time may lead to predictions of prostate cancer up to 10 years before clinical diagnosis of prostate cancer," Fozard said.

PSA is found in high concentration in semen, but it also leaks into the blood stream when the prostate enlarges. Part of the PSA binds to the protein ACT, and comparing the levels of free and bound PSA is the essence of the new test.

Men whose total PSA levels are high may have prostate cancer or a benignly enlarged prostate gland. Earlier studies have shown that the increase in total PSA over several years is one of the best indicators of the presence of prostate cancer, the scientists said.
Their research was published in the journal Urology.

In other research into prostate cancer in older men, scientists found that even normal levels of the male hormone androgen might boost levels of gene-damaging chemicals that have been linked to prostate cancer.

More research into the connection "could potentially provide information on how to regulate or prevent certain age- and hormone-associated diseases, including cancer," said a study published in the Jan. 1 issue of the Journal of the National Cancer Institute.

The study looked to explain the apparent tie between ageing, androgen, antioxidants -- which counteract unstable DNA-damaging chemicals -- and prostate cancer, the most commonly diagnosed tumour in American men.
It followed research last year that concluded men who had a diet rich in tomatoes, which have the powerful antioxidant lycopene, had a lower risk of cancer.
